solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Border enforcement chief, in case London's not as bad as Farage & co claim

definitions.text: London's not as bad as Farage & co claim
definitions.note: The definition is a claim about the answer rather than a synonym for it: read it as London's ___ is not as bad as Farage & co say, with the entry filling the gap.

indicators.note: The chief of a word is the letter standing at its head, so only the first letter of the word before it is taken.
In puts what has just been named inside the thing named next, so those letters go between the outer ones.

blocks.note: a crate is the wooden case goods travel in, and it opens up to take the letters below
the rim of a wheel or a plate is its border
the opening letter of that word

explanation.surface: Nigel Farage and friends insisting the capital has been overrun by lawlessness.
explanation.walkthrough: Border enforcement reads as immigration control and is an edge plus one initial, with no officer anywhere in the wordplay. Reform UK has made London's lawlessness a standing claim, and the clue is answering back.
explanation.definitionFit: A crime rate is the figure that measures how much crime a place has, and London's is the number those claims about the capital keep running into.

clue.text: Pence temporarily given immunity at last, which is more than sufficient

definitions.note: The answer is a noun of quantity and the definition an adjectival phrase: it is pointing at the everyday use in which 'that is plenty' says there is more there than the job needs.

indicators.note: What comes at last in a word is the letter it finishes on, so one letter is taken from the end of the word before it.

blocks.note: p is the coin on every British price tag
something handed over for a while and wanted back has been lent
the letter that word ends on

explanation.surface: Mike Pence handed immunity for the time being, and a verdict on how generous that is.
explanation.walkthrough: Pence is the vice-president in the sentence and small change in the wordplay, which is the whole of the misdirection. Immunity is a long word supplying a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Plenty is having more of something than you need, which is what more than sufficient says in the formal register.

clue.text: Funeral introduces new form of detention

indicators.note: To introduce something is to bring it in, so the letter named next goes inside the word standing before it.

blocks.note: an interment is a burial, the part of a funeral that puts the body in the ground
n is the standard short form of new

explanation.surface: A burial service ushering in some freshly invented way of locking people up.
explanation.walkthrough: Two long words that differ by one letter sit either side of the parse, which is what lets the surface talk about funerals and prisons in the same breath. New is an adjective in the sentence and a single letter in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Internment is holding people without charge or trial, usually in wartime, which is one recognised form of detention.

clue.text: Far-right broadcaster producing book soon about "Nationalism chiefly"

indicators.note: Something placed about another thing goes round the outside of it, so those letters close over what is put inside them.
The chief of a word is its opening letter, so only the head of the word beside it is used.

blocks.note: b is the usual short form of book
anon is the old word for shortly, as in see you anon
the letter that word begins on

explanation.surface: A broadcaster with a book about nationalism due out before long.
explanation.walkthrough: Steve Bannon ran Trump's 2016 campaign and now puts out the War Room podcast daily, which is the broadcasting the definition means. The quotation marks dress the last two words up as a title and hide an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Steve Bannon is the American agitator of the populist right whose show is his platform, so far-right broadcaster names him by the job he does now.

clue.text: Arse-over-tip police force's making arrest

indicators.note: Arse over tip is the printable form of arse over tit, head over heels, so the word it governs is stood on its head.

blocks.note: the Met is London's police force and the 's joins on as a fourth letter, the four then read from the end back to the front

explanation.surface: A police force going head over heels in the course of making an arrest.
explanation.walkthrough: Arrest is a noun the police make in the sentence and a verb in the answer, the one used of stopping a flow. The possessive apostrophe is not punctuation here but a letter the solver has to keep.
explanation.definitionFit: To stem something is to bring it to a halt — stem the bleeding, stem the tide — which is arrest in its stop-it-dead sense.

clue.text: Swinger's nude balls hidden by fruit

indicators.note: To balls something up is to make a mess of it, and a mess of those letters is what the clue is after.
What is hidden by something is inside it and out of sight, so the letters doing the hiding part and close over it.

blocks.note: the fruit is a plum, and it opens up after its first letter
the four letters of nude in a new order

explanation.surface: A partner-swapper's bare testicles tucked out of sight behind a piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: Balls is anatomy in the sentence and the verb to balls up in the parse, so the rudest word is the instruction. Swinger does the same double duty, since only one kind hangs under a clock.
explanation.definitionFit: A pendulum is the weighted rod that swings to and fro under a clock, so swinger names it by the one thing it exists to do.

clue.text: Chant "Trump's almost content"

indicators.note: The content of something is what sits inside it, so a run of letters within the words quoted is what is wanted.

blocks.note: five letters running straight on through those two words, the apostrophe stepped over as crossword spelling allows

explanation.surface: Trump declared to be very nearly satisfied with something.
explanation.walkthrough: Almost sits exactly where an instruction to dock a word of its last letter would sit, and supplies three of the letters instead. The apostrophe in the middle of the run is what makes it hard to see.
explanation.definitionFit: A psalm is one of the Psalter's sacred songs, delivered in church by chanting rather than singing, so chant names it by how it is performed.

clue.text: Tempting to switch sides, being a monarch

indicators.note: The sides are left and right, written l and r, and switching them puts each of those letters where the other one stood.

blocks.note: to tempt somebody on is to lure them

explanation.surface: A politician crossing the floor and ending up on the throne.
explanation.walkthrough: Switching sides is defection in the sentence and an exchange of two letters in the parse: the l and the r trade places and the other four never move.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch on the throne is ruling, the participle covering the whole business of reigning rather than any one act of it.

clue.text: Imprudent time to reduce the stage appearances

blocks.note: t is the standard short form of time
cutting down how often you go on stage is acting less, and the two words run together

explanation.surface: Telling a performer it is time they were seen on stage rather less often.
explanation.walkthrough: The long chunk is a plain instruction — act less — dressed as a comment on a fading career, and only the join between its two words does any hiding. Time gives up its usual single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody tactless says the thing better left unsaid, which is imprudent in the sense of lacking judgement rather than lacking caution.

clue.text: "Led astray in one of Epstein's homes? Not I" – ex-peer

indicators.note: In puts what has just been named inside the thing named next, so those letters go into the middle of it.
Not takes away what it names, so that letter is missing from the word it is set against.

blocks.note: the financier owned several houses, the New York one a mansion off Fifth Avenue
the letter stands for itself, and it is the one taken out of the house above
the three letters of led in a new order

explanation.surface: Somebody hotly denying that he was the one led into bad ways at an Epstein address.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks turn the wordplay into a denial, and Not I is a letter leaving a house rather than anyone protesting innocence. Peter Mandelson's dealings with Epstein are what cost him the ambassadorship in Washington.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Mandelson, sacked as ambassador to Washington, is the peer the government has pledged to strip of his title over the Epstein files, so the ex is awarded early.

clue.text: They come in twos, bashes

definitions.note: The first definition is a sentence about the things rather than a name for them, identifying them by the pair they are always sold and worn in.

blocks.note: one goes on each foot, and shops sell them by the pair
as a noun, bashes are hard blows with the fist

explanation.walkthrough: Bashes reads as parties on the way past and has to be taken as thumps. A comma is the only thing marking the seam between two definitions, which is what makes the first half read as scene-setting.
explanation.definitionFit: Socks are worn and sold in pairs, and a sock is also a heavy blow, so both halves land on the same plural.

clue.text: Head of Dept. involved in, say, Barbie award

indicators.note: The head of a word is the letter it starts with, here the shortened word that follows.
Something involved in a thing is caught up inside it, so that letter sits within the word named next.
Say marks what follows as one example of a wider thing, so it is the general word that the letters spell.

blocks.note: a barbie is Australian for a barbecue, which is one way of feeding people
the opening letter of the shortened word

explanation.surface: A departmental boss mixed up in some prize given to a Barbie doll.
explanation.walkthrough: Barbie is the doll in the sentence and the Australian barbecue in the wordplay, with say quietly promoting it to the general word. The full stop after Dept. belongs to the abbreviation, not to the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A medal is the struck disc pinned on for bravery or for winning, which is an award in the most literal sense of the word.

clue.text: Shaft our national leaders for fake material

indicators.note: The leaders of words are the letters standing at their front, one taken from each.

blocks.note: a shaft of sunlight is a ray of it
the opening letter of each of those two words

explanation.surface: Doing the country's leaders over in exchange for something counterfeit.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaft is the verb of the sentence, to do somebody down, and a noun of light in the parse. Our national leaders sounds like politicians and is two initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Rayon is the cellulose fibre sold for a century as artificial silk, so fake material names it by the cloth it stands in for.

clue.text: Mocking Clegg not quite fitting into lacy creation

indicators.note: Not quite the whole word means it stops one letter short of its end.
What fits into something goes inside it, so those letters are set within the ones around them.
A creation is something newly made, so the letters it is made from come out in a new arrangement.

blocks.note: the four letters of lacy reset, and they part to take the piece below
Nick Clegg led the Liberal Democrats and was deputy prime minister in the 2010 coalition
the last letter of that name goes, leaving it one short

explanation.surface: Poking fun at Nick Clegg squeezing himself into something made of lace.
explanation.walkthrough: Mocking sits where an anagram indicator would sit and is the definition; creation is what does the shuffling. Clegg is given by surname and answers with his first name, which is the step most solvers reach last.
explanation.definitionFit: A cynical remark sneers at anybody's good motives, which is mocking in its jeering sense rather than its imitating one.

clue.text: And Corbyn, pissed, stifles half-laugh – bastard's gone for a drink

indicators.note: Pissed is drunk, and a drunk's letters will not stay in the order they were given in.
To stifle something is to smother it, so what is stifled disappears inside the letters doing it.
What has gone is no longer there, so that letter is missing from the pile beside it.

blocks.note: those letters reset once the b below has left them, and they part after the first to let the next piece in
b is how a paper prints the word when it will not spell it out
a laugh written down is ha-ha, so half of one is a single ha

explanation.surface: A drunk Jeremy Corbyn swallowing a snigger as some swine heads off to the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-laugh is not half the letters of laugh: a laugh on the page is ha-ha, and half of that is one syllable. Pissed is the state of the man in the sentence and the instruction in the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: Chardonnay is the white grape and the wine pressed from it, so a drink is the general thing it is one particular instance of.

clue.text: Announcer POTUS put off ("No depth!")

indicators.note: No says the thing it names is absent, so that letter is missing from the word standing before it.

blocks.note: POTUS is the President of the United States, and the present holder is the paper's favourite subject
to put somebody off doing something is to deter them
d is the short form a plan or a chart uses for depth

explanation.surface: The president dismissing something as having no depth to it whatever.
explanation.walkthrough: No depth is a verdict in the sentence and an instruction in the parse, and the letter it removes is the one a drawing writes for depth. A trumpeter is the herald who sounds the fanfare when somebody grand arrives.
explanation.definitionFit: A trumpeter blows the fanfare that announces an arrival, so announcer names the man by the job rather than by his instrument.

clue.text: Semi-nude cast going round some place east

indicators.note: What goes round a thing stands on both sides of it, so those letters open up and enclose the rest.
Some of a word is part of it, here the part a street sign leaves when it shortens the word.

blocks.note: to cast a ball is to toss it, and the word opens after its second letter
pl. is how place is shortened on a street sign
e is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A half-dressed touring company playing somewhere out east.
explanation.walkthrough: Semi-nude looks like an instruction to strip a word of half its letters and is the definition. Cast is a verb of throwing here, not the company the surface assembles.
explanation.definitionFit: Topless is bare from the waist upward, which is semi-nude exactly: undressed, but only half of the way down.

clue.text: View of old Republican stuffing a foreign country

indicators.note: To stuff something into a thing is to cram it inside, so those letters sit in the middle of the word named next.

blocks.note: Panama is the Central American republic of the canal, foreign from a British desk
o is the standard short form of old
r is how the American party is shortened beside a result

explanation.surface: An elderly Republican cramming himself into a small foreign republic.
explanation.walkthrough: Panorama is the BBC's long-running current-affairs programme, so view of can be heard as a broadcast; the answer wants the plain word for a wide prospect. The country is named nowhere and has to be guessed from its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A panorama is the whole sweep of country visible from a high point, which is view taken at its widest.

clue.text: Many jerks ruin the country!

indicators.note: To jerk a thing is to shake it hard, and letters shaken hard land in a different order.

blocks.note: the four letters of many shaken into a new order
to mar something is to spoil it

explanation.surface: A crowd of idiots wrecking the nation between them.
explanation.walkthrough: Jerks reads as the noun for the idiots and works as the verb that shakes the letters, which is the one word doing two jobs. The country is the one formerly called Burma, under its generals since the coup of 2021.
explanation.definitionFit: Myanmar is the South East Asian state that was Burma, so the country is the general word the name answers to.

clue.text: Precocious girl turns up without changing

indicators.note: A word that turns up without changing reads the same from either end, so there is nothing to reverse — only a symmetry to spot.

blocks.note: the definition end: a small girl giving herself the airs of a grown woman

explanation.surface: A pert little girl arriving and behaving exactly as she always does.
explanation.walkthrough: Turns up promises a reversal and without changing takes it away again, because the letters already mirror themselves. Calling a small girl a madam is British and only half affectionate.
explanation.definitionFit: A bossy little girl who is knowing beyond her years gets called a madam in British usage, which is the precocious girl the clue means.

clue.text: "NO WAY IT'S MY IMMIGRATION TEAM!" Donald at first remarked

indicators.note: What comes at first is the opening letter of the name standing before it.

blocks.note: no way is a flat refusal, which is what the little negative does in three letters
ICE is Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the American agency running the deportation raids
the opening letter of the name

explanation.surface: Trump bellowing that the squad on the news has nothing to do with him.
explanation.walkthrough: The shouting capitals are surface noise and the agency's initials are standing in them in plain sight. Remarked is the definition in its older sense of taking note rather than of saying anything.
explanation.definitionFit: To remark something, in the sense the word keeps in writing, is to take note of it, which is what noticed says in the plainer register.

clue.text: see 26dn.
Delusion of Democrat: to have a following of many papers

indicators.note: Something with a following has things coming along behind it, so the letters named next take their place after the first one.

blocks.note: d is how the American party is shortened beside a candidate's name
a ream is five hundred sheets of paper

explanation.surface: A Democrat fantasising about having the whole press behind him.
explanation.walkthrough: Papers are newspapers in the sentence and sheets in the parse, with many turning them into the stationer's quantity. Delusion picks the unkind one of the answer's two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A dream in the sense of a fond belief with nothing behind it is a delusion, which is the harsh word for the same thing.

clue.text: Injured arse (raised pimple) – I must go for  a substitute

indicators.note: Injured letters have been knocked out of the order they were standing in.
In a down entry what is raised is read upward, so that word comes out from its last letter to its first.
What must go is taken away, so that letter is not in the word beside it.

blocks.note: the four letters of arse in a new order
a pimple is a zit, and it is read up the column here
the letter stands for itself, and it is the one that leaves the turned-round word above

explanation.surface: A damaged backside and a squeezed spot, and somebody standing down in favour of a stand-in.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed aside looks like scene-setting and holds the second half of the wordplay, which has to be turned round before a letter can leave it. Ersatz is German for replacement and reached English with the wartime substitutes it labelled.
explanation.definitionFit: An ersatz is the inferior stand-in for the real thing, as ersatz coffee was for coffee, and English keeps the noun as well as the adjective.

clue.text: Elected Conservative put on tights?

indicators.note: In a down entry what is put on something sits above it, so that letter goes in front of the rest.

blocks.note: c is the short form printed beside the party on a ballot paper
hose is the old collective word for stockings and tights

explanation.surface: A Tory who got into parliament and then pulled on a pair of tights.
explanation.walkthrough: Elected Conservative wants to be one phrase naming an MP, and the tense settles it: the definition is the past of a verb. The question mark concedes that tights are only one kind of hose.
explanation.definitionFit: To choose is to elect in the sense of settling on one option — the committee elected to wait — and both words are in the past tense.

clue.text: Group of wives shoot male

blocks.note: to shoot off somewhere is to hare off, going flat out
m is the standard short form of male

explanation.surface: A pack of wives taking aim at some man.
explanation.walkthrough: Shoot is a verb of speed here rather than of guns, and the animal it names is doing the running. The wives at the front are the definition, so no shooting survives into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A harem is the body of wives and concubines kept by one man, so group of wives names them collectively.

clue.text: (& 21ac.) Nick, coach has itch to back a leader on Trump's hate list

definitions.text: a leader on Trump's hate list

indicators.note: To back a thing is to turn it round, so those letters are read from the end to the front.

blocks.note: a nick cut into a doorframe is a mark scored on it
a railway coach is a carriage, shortened to car
an itch for something is a yen for it, turned round here

explanation.surface: Nick the coach itching to throw his weight behind a politician the president loathes.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Carney governed the Bank of England and now runs Canada, the country Trump keeps threatening to annex. Nick reads as the trainer's name and is a notch cut in wood.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Carney leads the country Trump talks of making the fifty-first state, which is what puts him among the leaders the president rails at.

clue.text: Recall miners messing with ICE

indicators.note: Something messed about with does not come out as it went in, so the letters change order.

blocks.note: six of the nine letters, waiting to be reordered
the American immigration agency, whose three letters join the pile

explanation.surface: Miners squaring up to the immigration enforcers.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals are the only sign that those three letters are raw material and not frozen water. Recall is a verb here, which is what stops it being the noun a manufacturer issues.
explanation.definitionFit: To reminisce is to dwell fondly on times past, which is recall in its remembering sense rather than its summoning-back one.

clue.text: Those commonly held back by tosser playing for the county

indicators.note: What is held by something is kept inside it, so those letters sit within the ones doing the holding.
In an across entry a piece written back is read from right to left, so its two letters come out the other way round.
Letters at play are not standing still, so they come out in a different arrangement.

blocks.note: the six letters of tosser reset, and they part after two to take the pair below
them shrinks to 'em in common speech, those is standing in for them, and the pair is then read the other way round

explanation.surface: A useless player turning out for the county side.
explanation.walkthrough: Tosser is the man spinning the coin at the start of a cricket match and the Eye's favourite insult, and either way it is only letters. Somerset is a county in south-west England with one of the eighteen first-class cricket clubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Somerset is the English county, and playing for the county is what its cricket club does, which is the reading the sports page would take.

clue.text: Shed attached to the French chateau

blocks.note: a snake sheds its skin, which is to cast it
the French for the, in its masculine form

explanation.surface: A garden shed tacked onto a French country house.
explanation.walkthrough: Shed is a verb here and not the thing at the bottom of the garden, with casting a skin the sense wanted. A chateau is the French country seat, often fortified and moated.
explanation.definitionFit: A chateau is the French castle or grand country seat, so the French word names the English building type outright.
